target_customer: Consumers who backed the glowing plant Kickstarter, later biotech customers for plant engineering services and novelty scented moss buyers
problem: Genetic engineering of plants was slow and costly. The company first tried to make a glowing plant, then offered plant engineering services, then pivoted to a scented moss product.
business_model: Consumer crowdfunded product, plant engineering services platform, novelty moss product sales

founders.name: Antony Evans
founders.background_notes: Per Wired he had no prior biology experience and attended Singularity University in 2011.

founders.name: Kyle Taylor
founders.background_notes: Described by Wired as a cofounder who left in early 2015.

technical_complexity.rationale: Making plants glow brightly enough was an unsolved problem. Wired reports the best Arabidopsis plants were barely visible in the dark and tobacco proved harder than expected.

defensibility.rationale: Little exclusive technology was shown, and the product was a novelty. The crowd funded brand was the main asset.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent moved on the glowing plant idea in the sources I opened.

market_need_then: Demand was shown by the 2013 Kickstarter, which raised 484013 dollars from 8433 orders against a 65000 dollar goal per Wired. Kickstarter later banned new synthetic biology projects.

branding.name_origin: Renamed from Glowing Plant to TAXA, with the reason not stated in sources I opened

identity.logo: The Kickstarter campaign used an image from a 1986 Science paper as its logo, per Scientific American

rebrands.why: Not stated in sources; SynBioBeta in April 2015 asked whether the rename reflected a new product or a new company

branding.community_and_virality: A Kickstarter with 8433 orders and heavy press, plus a Wefunder campaign with over 500 investors in 2016.

brand_strength.rationale: The Glowing Plant brand drove national press and crowdfunding, but the promised product never shipped and the later TAXA name had little recognition.

pivots.why: Platform sold protein engineering, DNA assembly and plant transformation as a service per the YC page
Moss is simpler than Arabidopsis and needs one gene change to alter scent, per Wired

outcome_analysis: The company raised about half a million dollars on Kickstarter and 120000 from YC but could not make plants glow brightly, and money ran short while cofounder Kyle Taylor left in early 2015. It pivoted to scented moss and a services platform, raised about 300000 on Wefunder in 2016, and missed its March 2017 moss ship date after contamination. Final status is not confirmed, and the YC directory lists it inactive.
notes: YC website is not listed and no company site was fetched. The Wired text was read through a mirror page whose publication date is not shown. The Kickstarter predates YC and is kept as a round flagged other. The 2016 Wefunder amount of 309807 comes from a search snippet of the Wefunder page, while the GlobeNewswire headline says 250000 at campaign close, and Wired says about 300000. Dealroom lists seeds of 480k, 430k and 125k and CB Insights a 1.26M total, which do not reconcile, and a university case study says 752807 in crowdfunding by 2016. The Scientist reported unnamed seed venture backing. No dated competitor was found, so the list is empty. YC page also names Dr Kyle Taylor as a founder profile. Whether the company closed is unconfirmed, so exit is unknown.
